title: Harness Memory: How to Build Persistent AI Agent Context
summary: Recursive architectures allow developers to harness memory for long-running autonomous agents. You can implement these structures to retain context.
body_markdown:
## Connecting harness memory to your existing automated workflows


Because the platform does not yet offer a native, pre-built integration, connecting Harness Memory to your current stack requires using standard API building blocks. While native connectors simplify setup, leveraging the underlying REST architecture ensures your memory layer remains portable across different automation engines.


### Using the HTTP request step for memory retrieval


By configuring a standard POST request to your memory node, you bridge the gap between volatile model context and persistent storage.


When I first tried to sync a long-running research agent, the agent would lose the thread of previous PDF summaries.


By routing every summary through a dedicated memory endpoint, the agent can query its own history as a structured JSON object. The following sequence establishes this persistent link:


1. Deploy the Harness-Memory Node package to your environment.
2. Initialize the instance with the bootstrap command to generate your unique API keys.
3. Create an HTTP Request step within your automation flow.
4. Map the 'Evidence Consolidation' flow to ensure new data is indexed immediately.
5. Set manual review or promote triggers to prevent low-quality hallucinations from entering the permanent memory tier.


This manual mapping forces you to define exactly which data points are worth remembering, rather than storing irrelevant chat logs. It's a necessary step.


Activepieces provides a built-in Knowledge Base and Tables that can be exposed as tools for any agent to query.


By registering these as tool schemas on the platform's per-project MCP server, integrations can be reached by models like Claude or GPT as native capabilities.


This ensures that the same data used in a deterministic flow is available to an agent's reasoning loop without maintaining a separate catalog, as every integration action effectively functions as an agent tool.


### Setting up OpenAI-compatible model endpoints


Standardizing your memory access via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint allows you to swap between different high-reasoning models without rewriting your entire prompt library.


Pointing a workflow at a Harness-hosted proxy allowed me to test Claude Fable 5.2 for complex reasoning alongside Gemini 4 Carbon for heavy data processing.


This setup maintained a single source of truth for the agent’s memory.


Because Harness Memory presents itself as a standard chat completion target, you can drop its URL into the Base URL field of any provider-agnostic AI step.


This configuration ensures that your agent sees the Memory as just another participant in the conversation, allowing it to pull past facts as if they were part of the immediate system prompt. It's seamless.


### Integrating via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers


Implementing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server creates a standardized bridge that allows local tools and remote memory to communicate without custom glue code.


When I hooked GPT-6 Astra into a local file system via MCP, the agent could read my code and query the Harness Memory server. It could see why specific architectural choices were made three weeks prior.


By running a dedicated MCP server for Harness, you expose your persistent memory as a Resource or Tool that the model can call natively.


This setup moves the responsibility of memory retrieval away from the automation logic and into the model’s own reasoning loop, resulting in more fluid transitions between current tasks and historical data. It's a better workflow.
